title: transporting dangerous goods
objectives: List the nine classes of dangerous goods
Explain the requirements for placards, shipping documents and route signs
State the driver's responsibilities for training, certification and incident reporting

sections.title: what counts as dangerous goods: classes, placards and documents
points: Dangerous goods present a serious potential hazard to handlers, the public and the environment.
There are nine classes, from Class 1 explosives through Class 9 miscellaneous products, substances or organisms.
Placards appear on the sides and both ends of transport trucks; a mixed-load placard exists for combined shipments.
Shipping documents must be complete, correct, readily available in the cab and accompany the shipment.
Some road signs designate routes where dangerous goods vehicles may travel; others prohibit them.
mustKnow: The nine classes: explosives, gases, flammable liquids, flammable solids, oxidizing substances and organic peroxides, poisonous and infectious substances, radioactive materials, corrosive substances, and miscellaneous products or substances.
Shipping documents must be complete, correct and readily available in the cab.

check.q: How many classes of dangerous goods are there?
check.explanation: There are nine classes of dangerous goods, from explosives to miscellaneous products or substances.

check.q: Where must shipping documents be kept when transporting dangerous goods?
choices: Filed at the carrier's head office
Attached to the outside of the trailer
check.explanation: Shipping documents must be complete, correct and readily available in the cab, accompanying the shipment.

sections.title: driver responsibilities: training, certification and reporting
points: Anyone working with dangerous goods has significant legal responsibilities and must be properly trained and appropriately certified.
Your current employer must certify that you've had appropriate dangerous goods training.
Always carry your training certificate with you when transporting dangerous goods.
Report immediately any incident — spills, leaks, fires, explosions or damaged containers — to the nearest police or the Provincial Emergency Program.
Rapid action after an incident may help prevent it from becoming serious.
mustKnow: Report dangerous goods incidents in B.C. immediately by calling local police or the Provincial Emergency Program at 1-800-663-3456.
Your current employer must certify your training, and you must carry your training certificate when transporting dangerous goods.

check.q: Who must certify that you've had appropriate dangerous goods training?
check.explanation: Your current employer must certify your training, and you must carry the certificate while transporting dangerous goods.

check.q: What should you do if your dangerous goods cargo leaks or spills?
choices: Finish the trip, then file a report
Wait 24 hours to see if it worsens
Report immediately to the nearest police or the Provincial Emergency Program
check.explanation: Report any incident immediately to the nearest police agency or the Provincial Emergency Program at 1-800-663-3456.

summary: There are nine classes of dangerous goods, shown on placards on the sides and both ends of transport trucks.
Shipping documents must be complete, correct and readily available in the cab with the shipment.
You must be trained, certified by your current employer, and carry your training certificate when transporting dangerous goods.
Report any incident — spill, leak, fire, explosion or damaged container — immediately to police or the Provincial Emergency Program at 1-800-663-3456.
